assessment.title: Final Comprehensive Assessment A1–C2
assessment.description: A complete end-of-course evaluation across all six CEFR-aligned platform levels, with final level estimation, skill analysis, review signals, and an initial-to-final comparison when a diagnostic result is available.
assessment.instructions: Complete all six stages from A1 through C2. Each stage contains 12 questions. Listening passages may be played a maximum of two times. Stage scores remain hidden until the complete final report.

questions.prompt: Complete: My sister ___ a teacher.
questions.explanation: Use 'is' with singular third-person subjects.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: Present simple takes -s with he/she/it.

questions.prompt: Complete: We ___ dinner right now.
questions.explanation: Present continuous describes an action happening now.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is a polite greeting?
questions.explanation: 'Good morning' is a standard greeting.

questions.prompt: Complete: The meeting is ___ Monday.
questions.explanation: Use 'on' with days of the week.

questions.prompt: Which sentence expresses ability?
questions.explanation: Can + base verb expresses ability.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct question.
questions.explanation: Past simple questions use did + base verb.

questions.prompt: Complete: They are going to ___ a new apartment.
questions.explanation: Use the base verb after going to.

questions.prompt: Complete: I have never ___ that film.
questions.explanation: Present perfect uses the past participle.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct comparative.
questions.explanation: The comparative of 'cheap' is 'cheaper'.

questions.prompt: What does 'get off the train' mean?
questions.explanation: Get off means leave a vehicle.

questions.prompt: Which sentence gives advice?
questions.explanation: Should is used for advice.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.option_c: I have finish the report yesterday.
questions.option_d: I did finished the report yesterday.
questions.explanation: A finished past time takes past simple.

questions.prompt: Complete: If the weather ___ good, we'll eat outside.
questions.explanation: First conditional uses present simple in the if-clause.

questions.prompt: If I ___ more time, I'd learn another language.
questions.explanation: Second conditional uses past simple in the if-clause.

questions.prompt: What does 'look into a problem' mean?
questions.explanation: Look into means investigate.

questions.prompt: Which linker expresses contrast?
questions.explanation: However introduces contrast.

questions.prompt: Which sentence means attendance is optional?
questions.explanation: Don't have to means there is no obligation.

questions.prompt: If we ___ the warning, we wouldn't have lost the data.
questions.explanation: Third conditional uses past perfect in the condition.

questions.prompt: The office is empty. Everyone ___ home.
questions.explanation: Must have + participle expresses strong past deduction.

questions.prompt: The system ___ at the moment.
questions.explanation: Present continuous passive is required.

questions.prompt: What does 'turn down an offer' mean?
questions.explanation: Turn down means reject.

questions.prompt: Which connector means 'despite that'?
questions.explanation: Nevertheless signals contrast despite the previous point.

questions.prompt: Choose the natural collocation.
questions.explanation: Take responsibility is the standard collocation.

questions.prompt: Not until the review ended ___ the extent of the problem.
questions.explanation: Not until triggers inversion.

questions.prompt: ___ the evidence, the committee revised its position.
questions.explanation: The perfect participle shows prior completion.

questions.prompt: The company is believed ___ the option last month.
questions.explanation: The perfect infinitive reports an earlier action.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is most appropriately hedged?
questions.option_a: The evidence appears to support the claim.
questions.option_b: The evidence proves the claim absolutely.
questions.explanation: Appears to is a cautious stance marker.

questions.prompt: What does 'a grey area' mean?
questions.explanation: A grey area is unclear or not fully defined.

questions.prompt: What does 'I'm not entirely convinced' usually signal?
questions.explanation: The phrase softens disagreement.

questions.prompt: In 'The results should be available tomorrow,' 'should' primarily expresses...
questions.explanation: At this level, should can express expected probability.

questions.prompt: She predicted the system would fail, and ___ it did.
questions.explanation: 'So it did' confirms the prediction emphatically.

questions.prompt: Which paraphrase preserves the stance of 'The findings may indicate a modest effect'?
questions.option_a: The findings point to a possible small effect.
questions.option_b: The findings prove a major effect.
questions.explanation: Both uncertainty and degree are preserved.

questions.prompt: Which word best describes a limiting factor that does not make action impossible?
questions.explanation: A constraint restricts options without necessarily blocking them.

questions.prompt: After a major failure, 'That could have gone better' is most likely...
questions.explanation: The phrase minimizes the severity for rhetorical effect.

questions.prompt: What methodological issue can a voluntary survey create?
questions.explanation: Volunteers may differ systematically from non-respondents.

passages.title: A Simple Weekday
passages.instructions: Read the text and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What time does Emma get up?
questions.explanation: She gets up at seven.

questions.prompt: How does she travel to work?
questions.explanation: She takes the bus.

questions.prompt: What does she always do before bed?
questions.explanation: She always reads for twenty minutes.

passages.content_text: Emma gets up at seven every weekday. She has breakfast at home and takes the bus to work at eight. She works in a small office until five. After work, she usually buys food and then goes home. In the evening, she sometimes watches a series, but she always reads for twenty minutes before bed.

passages.title: At a Café
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions. You may play it twice.

questions.prompt: What food does the customer order?
questions.explanation: The customer orders a chicken sandwich.

questions.prompt: What drink is ordered besides water?
questions.explanation: A small coffee is ordered.

questions.prompt: How much is the order?
questions.explanation: The total is twelve dollars.

passages.audio_text: Good afternoon. Can I have a chicken sandwich and a bottle of water, please? Of course. Would you like anything else? Yes, a small coffee, please. That's twelve dollars altogether.

passages.title: A Weekend in the City
passages.instructions: Read the text and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: How did Sofia travel?
questions.explanation: They took an early train.

questions.prompt: Why did they go to a museum on Sunday?
questions.explanation: Rain changed their plan.

questions.prompt: When did they return home?
questions.explanation: They returned Sunday evening.

passages.content_text: Last weekend, Sofia went to a nearby city with two friends. They took an early train on Saturday and arrived before nine. First, they visited an outdoor market and bought some local food. In the afternoon, they walked through the old town and took many photos. It rained on Sunday morning, so they went to a museum instead of the park. They returned home in the evening.

passages.title: Station Information
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions. You may play it twice.

questions.prompt: Which platform is used?
questions.explanation: The train leaves from platform four.

questions.prompt: Is the service direct?
questions.explanation: The announcement says it is direct.

questions.prompt: When should passengers be on the platform?
questions.explanation: Passengers should arrive at least five minutes before departure.

passages.audio_text: The train to Bristol leaves from platform four at eleven twenty. It is a direct service and arrives at twelve forty-five. Passengers should be on the platform at least five minutes before departure.

passages.title: A Change of Plans
passages.instructions: Read the text and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: Why did Martin decide to go?
questions.option_a: He had already finished his work
questions.explanation: He had finished his work.

questions.prompt: What fixed arrangement has been made?
questions.explanation: The meeting time is arranged.

questions.prompt: What will Martin do if trains are still running?
questions.explanation: The first conditional states the plan.

passages.content_text: Martin had planned to spend Friday evening at home, but a colleague invited him to a concert. He had already finished his work for the week, so he decided to go. They are meeting outside the venue at seven. Martin is going to take the train because parking is expensive in the city center. He thinks the concert will finish around ten thirty, and if the trains are still running, he will travel home immediately afterward.

passages.title: Team Discussion
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions. You may play it twice.

questions.prompt: Why is a new deadline proposed?
questions.explanation: Testing took longer than expected.

questions.prompt: What should happen today?
questions.explanation: The client should be told today.

questions.prompt: What will Friday be used for if the change is accepted?
questions.explanation: Friday will be used for final checks.

passages.audio_text: I think we should move the deadline to Monday because testing has taken longer than expected. I agree we need more time; however, we should tell the client today and explain the reason clearly. If they accept the change, we'll use Friday for final checks.

passages.title: A Hybrid Policy Review
passages.instructions: Read the text and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What has increased according to surveys?
questions.explanation: Surveys show higher satisfaction.

questions.prompt: What problem do managers identify?
questions.explanation: Onboarding is described as more difficult.

questions.prompt: What compromise is being considered?
questions.explanation: Two fixed office days are proposed.

passages.content_text: A company introduced a hybrid policy eighteen months ago. Employee surveys suggest that satisfaction has increased, particularly among staff with long commutes. Productivity measures have remained broadly stable. Nevertheless, managers report that onboarding new employees has become more difficult because informal support happens less often. The company is therefore considering two fixed office days each week. This would preserve flexibility while creating regular opportunities for collaboration. Critics argue that fixed days reduce individual choice, whereas supporters say coordination has become too difficult under the current system.

passages.title: Possible Cause
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions. You may play it twice.

questions.prompt: What may have contributed to the problem?
questions.explanation: The update is considered a plausible cause.

questions.prompt: Why can't the update be the only cause?
questions.option_a: An unchanged service was also affected
questions.explanation: One affected service was not changed.

questions.prompt: What should happen before a conclusion is drawn?
questions.explanation: The speaker wants more evidence.

passages.audio_text: The server became unstable shortly after the update, so the update may well have contributed to the problem. However, it can't have been the only cause because one of the affected services wasn't changed at all. We need to check the network logs before we draw a conclusion.

passages.title: Evaluating a Policy Argument
passages.instructions: Read the text and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What concern do critics raise?
questions.explanation: Additional approvals may slow urgent cases.

questions.prompt: How does the writer respond?
questions.option_a: Suggests a proportional exception rather than rejecting oversight
questions.explanation: The response proposes an accelerated route.

questions.prompt: Why should savings claims remain cautious?
questions.explanation: The evidence base is limited.

passages.content_text: Supporters of the new procurement rule argue that centralized purchasing will reduce duplication and strengthen oversight. Critics contend that the policy may also slow urgent purchases by requiring additional approvals. That concern is credible, particularly for small operational teams. However, it does not necessarily follow that decentralization is preferable. A more proportionate response may be to retain centralized oversight while creating an accelerated route for genuinely urgent cases. The evidence currently available is limited, so claims about the policy's long-term savings should remain cautious.

passages.title: Cautious Interpretation
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions. You may play it twice.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker's stance?
questions.explanation: The speaker recognizes improvement but withholds a strong conclusion.

questions.prompt: Why is the increase difficult to interpret?
questions.option_a: One major contract explains a large part
questions.explanation: The result may be concentrated in one contract.

questions.prompt: What evidence does the speaker want next?
questions.explanation: Continuation would strengthen the recovery interpretation.

passages.audio_text: The latest figures are encouraging, but I'd hesitate to call this a recovery yet. Sales improved for two consecutive months, which is clearly positive. Still, one major contract accounts for a substantial part of the increase, so we need to see whether the trend continues without that effect.

passages.title: A Strong Headline, a Weaker Design
passages.instructions: Read the text and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What major design limitation is identified?
questions.explanation: The design cannot separate software and training effects.

questions.prompt: What additional sampling issue exists?
questions.option_c: There were too many control groups
questions.explanation: Voluntary participation may introduce self-selection.

questions.prompt: What conclusion is most defensible?
questions.option_a: The 20% figure is an observed association, not a precise causal estimate
questions.option_b: The software definitely causes a 20% improvement
questions.explanation: The evidence supports a cautious associative interpretation.

passages.content_text: A report claims that organizations using a new analytics platform make decisions 20 percent faster. The number is impressive, but the study compares current customers before and after a training program without including a comparable group that received training but not the platform. Participants also volunteered to provide performance data. The report therefore cannot isolate the effect of the software from the effect of training, repeated practice, or self-selection. None of this shows that the platform is ineffective. It does mean, however, that the headline figure should be treated as an association observed in a particular sample rather than as a precise causal estimate.

passages.title: Integrated Evaluation
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions. You may play it twice.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker's main reservation?
questions.option_a: The causal claim is too strong
questions.explanation: The speaker questions attribution, not the whole proposal.

questions.prompt: Why is causality uncertain?
questions.option_a: Staffing changes occurred at the same time
questions.explanation: Concurrent changes create alternative explanations.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker recommend?
questions.option_a: Narrow the claim and run a larger evaluation
questions.explanation: The recommendation aligns the claim with the evidence.

passages.audio_text: The proposal is persuasive and the projected benefits are plausible. Where I'd be more cautious is the causal claim. The pilot shows that processing time fell after the new system was introduced, but several staffing changes occurred at the same time. So I wouldn't reject the proposal; I'd narrow the claim and recommend a larger evaluation before attributing the improvement primarily to the technology.
